To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the CD4+ T cell count, CD4+ T-cell percentage and the CD4/CD8 ratio are the most important parameters for predicting HIV disease progression.

the use of a statistical model to analyze the data is not only a useful tool for understanding the relationship between HIV-1-specific cytotoxic T-lymphocytes (CTL) and the immune system, but also for predicting the outcome of HIV infection.

the use of a new, more sensitive, and specific method to measure the HIV-specific CD8+ T-cell responses in patients with HIV infection was associated with a lower plasma HIV viral load, a higher CD4+ T-cell count, and a CD8+ T-lymphocytes that are CD38- and HLA-DR-.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new class of HIV-1 inhibitors, which we have termed "dual inhibitors".
the measurement of HIV-1-specific CTL activity in HIV-infected individuals.
the development of novel methods and techniques to study the dynamics of complex systems.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the HIV-1-specific cytotoxic T-lymphocytes are associated with lower viral load and higher CD4 count.
the HIV-1 specific cytolytic T lymphocyte activity is a strong predictor of lower viral loads, higher CD4 counts and CD8+ CD38+DR- phenotype.
the HIV-1-specific cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL) responses are associated with the lower viral load, the higher CD4 count and the CD8+ CD38- DR-.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have demonstrated that HIV-1-specific CTL activity is associated with a lower viral load, a higher CD4 count and a higher proportion of CD8+CD28+ cells and a lower percentage of CD8+DR+ cells, and that the CD38-DR- subset of cells may be the most relevant in terms of CTL activity.

we have demonstrated that HIV-1-specific CD8+ cytolytic T-cell (CTL) activity is associated with lower viral load (VL) and higher CD4 count in a cohort of chronically infected patients and that this association is independent of CD4 count and CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell activation.

we have developed a new method for measuring the activity of HIV-1-specific cytotoxic T-lymphocytes (CTL) in the peripheral blood of HIV-infected patients and that this method correlates with the clinical status of these patients.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the CD8+CD28+ T-cell population is a major source of IFN-gamma production in response to HIV-1 infection, and the CD8+ CD28- population may be an important source of TNF-alpha production.

there is a strong association between CD4+ T cell count and viral load, and that this association is stronger for people with a CD4+ T count above 500 cells/mm(3) than for those with a count below 500 cells/mm (3).
we can use the data from a clinical study to predict how a patient's immune system will respond to an experimental HIV vaccine.
